did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens with a call for the LORD to appear as the God of vengeance and judge of the earth. The repetition of the phrase “God of vengeance” emphasizes the psalmist’s plea for divine intervention against injustice.

Did you know? The psalmist describes the oppressors as harming “your people” and “your heritage”—that is, the LORD’s people and community. In this way, injustice is presented not only as harm against human beings, but also as an attack on what belongs to the LORD.
Did you know? The widow, the foreigner, and the fatherless are mentioned as examples of vulnerable people whom the wicked abuse. Mentioning them highlights the seriousness of the moral injustice.
Did you know? The wicked claim that the LORD does not see or understand what they are doing. This claim provides the starting point for the criticism the psalmist directs at them later.
Did you know? Through rhetorical questions about the ear and the eye, the psalmist argues that the one who created human senses must surely be able to hear and see what is happening.
Did you know? The LORD is described both as one who disciplines or corrects nations and as one who teaches people knowledge. The verse connects judgment, education, and understanding.
Did you know? The psalm declares that the LORD knows human thoughts and concludes that these thoughts are “vanity”—that is, unstable or of no use compared with the LORD’s knowledge.

Did you know? According to the psalm, the person who is disciplined and taught from the LORD’s law is blessed. Here, suffering is presented in the context of correction, learning, and guidance, rather than merely as pain.

Did you know? In the midst of the description of the wicked, a central promise appears: the LORD will not reject his people or abandon his heritage. This promise explains the psalmist’s hope even when justice is not yet visible.

Did you know? The psalmist describes his condition using the image of a foot nearly slipping, and immediately adds that the LORD’s steadfast love supports him. In this way, divine help is presented as support in a moment of weakness.
